Golomb's Tromino Theorem

InductionCountingArea

Puzzle by Alexander Bogomolny (cut-the-knot.org)

What it shows: One square is missing from a square board, and L-shaped pieces of three squares fill all the others.
How to play: Click a square to move the gap, then press One step to fill one more round. Choose a bigger size to see the same idea on a larger board.

Look for the math

A square board of size 2n × 2n has one square taken away. Remarkably, the rest can always be covered exactly by L-trominoes — three unit squares in an L — wherever that missing square happens to be. The applet shows Solomon Golomb's proof one layer at a time.

The idea: cut into four

Draw the two middle lines. They split the board into four equal smaller boards. The missing square lies in exactly one of them. Put a single L-tromino around the centre so that it covers one centre square in each of the other three boards. Now every one of the four smaller boards has a square missing — the original one in one board, a fresh one from the centre L in the other three.

Why it always works

Each smaller board has the same problem as the big one, just half the width. Do the same cut again, and again. This is mathematical induction: if the trick works for a 2 × 2 board, and doing it once turns any board into smaller boards of the same kind, it works for every size. The smallest case is a 2 × 2 board with one square gone — the three left over are exactly one L-tromino, so the process stops there. The L-tromino is a rep-tile: four smaller copies make a bigger one.

How many pieces?

A 2n × 2n board has 4n squares. With one missing, there are 4n − 1 to cover, and each L uses 3, so the number of pieces is (4n − 1) / 3. The logic test checks every missing square on boards up to 16 × 16: the pieces never overlap, they never touch the hole, they cover every other square once, and that formula always gives their count. For the default 16 × 16 board it is (256 − 1) / 3 = 85 pieces, all placed after four presses of One step.

Try the same missing square at different sizes: watch how the first L always goes round the middle, and the later ones repeat the picture in each quarter.
